extensions: Run a 48-hour pre-launch soft-access campaign with 20–50 real users (beta list, Discord, personal network) and gate their access on leaving a verified review — this generates authentic social proof before the public listing goes live, solving the cold-start problem without fraud.

Use a 'review incentive ladder': offer a legitimate post-purchase discount code for a future order in exchange for an honest review, disclosed per FTC guidelines — this converts early buyers into reviewers at a cost of ~10–15% margin rather than risking platform delisting.

Submit to press and independent review sites (Product Hunt, G2, Capterra, relevant niche blogs) before launch day, so that third-party coverage links and quotes can be featured on the product listing as social proof even when on-platform reviews are zero.
nonObviousAngles: The 'zero review' problem is a symptom of a distribution problem, not a credibility problem: if the launch audience is large enough, reviews arrive within hours. The impulse to fake reviews reveals that the launch audience is too small.

Every major marketplace has invested heavily in fake-review detection using behavioural signals, NLP fingerprinting, and account graph analysis — AI-generated text is now a primary signal. Detection probability on launch day, when the account has no prior review history, is significantly higher than teams estimate.

If this idea succeeds in the narrow sense — reviews go undetected — it creates a permanent ongoing liability: the fake reviews sit on the listing indefinitely, each one a documented instance of consumer fraud that can be surfaced in litigation or press coverage at any future point.

weaknesses.text: The plan is illegal as stated. The FTC's updated rules on fake reviews (effective August 2024) treat AI-generated reviews as deceptive endorsements with civil penalties up to $51,744 per violation — each fake review is a separate violation. The UK's Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 similarly criminalises fake review commissioning. The EU Omnibus Directive is in force with active enforcement. Five fake reviews carries exposure up to $258,720 before any criminal referral.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The assumption that platform detection systems will not flag AI-generated reviews from a new account on launch day is almost certainly false. Amazon's Project Zero, Trustpilot's fraud detection, and Google's spam classifiers flag reviews posted in a burst near product creation date, from accounts with no review history, with stylistic consistency (an LLM signature). A five-review burst on day one hits three or four signals simultaneously. Detection does not merely remove reviews — it can result in listing suppression or account suspension.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The 'dilution plan' is strategically incoherent. Fake reviews do not become retroactively legitimate over time. If flagged six months later, every fake review posted on launch day is still evidence of deceptive practice. Early reviews carry disproportionate algorithmic weight — they determine initial ranking signals and rating baselines — meaning the fake reviews may have influenced thousands of purchase decisions before dilution occurs, each an actionable deceptive practice.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The reputational exposure is asymmetric and irreversible. A journalist, competitor, or platform audit discovering AI-generated fake reviews on launch day produces a news cycle that permanently associates the brand with fraud at the exact moment brand identity is being established. Startup brands have been permanently destroyed by review fraud stories. A launch-day brand has no goodwill to absorb the blow.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The opportunity cost of pursuing this path — even briefly before abandoning it — is that the team does not execute legitimate cold-start strategies that require lead time. A pre-launch soft-access review gate requires 4–6 weeks of planning. If the team deliberates for two weeks, that lead time is gone and launch day arrives with zero reviews regardless.
weaknesses.label: resolvable

risks: Platform account suspension or listing removal on launch day — the worst-case scenario occurs at the highest-stakes moment, with no recovery window before the launch marketing spend has already gone out.
Regulatory action initiated by a competitor filing an FTC complaint — competitors actively monitor new entrants and fake review detection is a low-cost, high-damage offensive move.
Internal knowledge of the practice becoming a liability — anyone who implemented this becomes a witness in regulatory proceedings, and internal communications discussing it are discoverable.
Rating baseline corruption — if fake reviews skew the initial rating upward and real reviews regress it, the rating visibly declines shortly after launch, signalling quality problems.
failureModes: Platform flags the review burst on launch day, suppresses the listing, and the team's launch marketing directs traffic to a suppressed listing — the launch generates paid traffic with no conversion surface and the spend is unrecoverable.

A journalist or competitor screenshots the AI-generated reviews before dilution, publishes a 'brand caught faking reviews on day one' story, and the brand becomes permanently associated with deception.

The team implements the plan, achieves the intended effect, then faces an FTC civil investigative demand 18 months later when the company has grown — at scale, the original five reviews influenced thousands of transactions, each a separate violation.

userChallenges: The actual end user of this idea is the product team launching a product — and their core problem (launch-day review anxiety) is real. However, the fake review 'solution' creates a second user class: the consumer who reads those reviews to make a purchase decision. That consumer is being actively harmed. When they discover the product does not match the social proof they relied on, trust damage falls on the brand permanently. Return rates, chargebacks, and public social media complaints are the measurable downstream costs the proposer's mental model excludes.

The Builder's legitimate extension — a pre-launch soft-access campaign gated on verified reviews — requires 20–50 real users willing to try an unproven product, write a review, and do so within 48 hours. This behaviour pattern exists only in communities where the founder already has warm relationships. A founder who has that network does not have a launch-day social proof problem. The extension solves the problem only for the person who least needs it.
adoptionRisks: Consumer-side fake review detection is now mainstream: browser extensions such as Fakespot and ReviewMeta are used by millions of shoppers on Amazon. A cluster of reviews posted from new accounts within 48 hours, with similar sentiment patterns and AI-generated linguistic signatures, will be flagged by these tools and displayed to consumers as 'suspicious' before any platform action is taken. The product gets a worse first impression than zero reviews.

The FTC-compliant discount-code incentive ladder the Builder proposes carries its own adoption friction: sellers must disclose the incentive, which consumers treat as a trust signal reduction. A disclosed incentivised review reads as 'they paid someone to say this' — it trades one form of reduced credibility for another that is legal but only marginally more persuasive.

strengths: The pre-launch soft-access campaign (Builder extension 1) solves the cold-start problem legitimately and produces verifiable reviews that survive platform audits.

Third-party press and review site coverage (Builder extension 3) is fully legitimate and often more credible than anonymous on-platform reviews — it creates social proof without touching the review system at all.
The underlying problem (zero reviews at launch suppresses conversion) is real, measurable, and solvable — the issue is only with this specific proposed solution.
suggestedPivots: Abandon fake reviews entirely; execute the pre-launch soft-access gate immediately since it requires 4–6 weeks lead time that is being consumed by deliberation.
Redirect launch budget toward press outreach and community seeding — third-party coverage achieves social proof without creating any platform or regulatory exposure.
Test whether zero reviews actually suppresses conversion for this specific product category before committing any resource to a social proof strategy.
openQuestions: What is the actual conversion rate differential between zero reviews and five reviews in this specific product category and platform? The assumption that zero reviews is catastrophically bad may itself be unvalidated.
Does the team have an existing warm-audience list of 20–50 people who could participate in a pre-launch soft-access review programme if started immediately?
Has the team assessed the FTC's August 2024 fake review rules and understood that each individual fake review is a separate civil violation?
